"À la carte" describes a system where you select individual items from a list of separate options, with each item carrying its own separate price or value, rather than receiving a fixed, pre-packaged combination.
Understanding it through a restaurant (the clearest way)

Picture walking into a restaurant that gives you two choices for how to order.

In the first option, you pay a single fixed price, and the restaurant hands you a pre-decided set — a starter, a main course, and a dessert. You don't get to pick. You take the whole package as it is.

In the second option, there's a long list of dishes. Each dish has its own price printed next to it. You browse the list and pick exactly what you want — maybe just a main course, maybe two starters and no dessert, maybe everything on the list. Your bill is the sum of whatever you individually chose.

That second option is the à la carte system. The menu is called an à la carte menu, and the way of ordering is called ordering à la carte.
The two ideas always at the heart of this word

Whenever something is described as "à la carte," two things are always true. First, there is individual selection — you choose items one by one from a list, rather than accepting a pre-set bundle. Second, there is individual pricing — each item you pick carries its own separate cost or value, rather than everything being lumped into one fixed price.

Strip away the restaurant setting and those two ideas are what "à la carte" always means, no matter where you see it used.
How the word lives outside restaurants

This is where the word gets truly interesting, because today "à la carte" is used far beyond food. Any system that works like that restaurant menu — where you pick and pay for individual pieces instead of a fixed bundle — can be called à la carte.

A cable or streaming provider that lets you subscribe only to the specific channels you actually want, instead of forcing you to buy a full pre-packaged bundle of hundreds of channels, is offering à la carte television. A software company that lets you pay only for the individual features you need, rather than buying the entire software suite, is offering à la carte pricing. A university that allows students to register for single courses without committing to a full degree program is offering à la carte enrollment. A wedding photographer who prices photography, an album, and prints as three completely separate services rather than one fixed wedding package is operating on an à la carte model.

In every single one of these cases, the word is doing exactly the same job — pointing to a system built around individual choice and individual pricing.

When you call something "à la carte," you are signaling several things at once. You are signaling flexibility, because the person gets to decide what they want rather than accepting someone else's decision. You are signaling personalization, because different people can walk away with completely different combinations based on their own needs. You are signaling the absence of forced bundling, meaning nobody has to pay for or receive something they didn't ask for.

There is also one important trade-off that comes up frequently in the real world: à la carte options are often more expensive per individual item than if you had bought them as part of a bundle. This is because the provider charges a premium for the convenience and freedom of letting you choose. So while à la carte gives you more control, it does not always give you the cheapest total cost — especially if you end up choosing many items.
How it functions grammatically as an adjective

As an adjective, "à la carte" describes a noun. It can sit directly in front of the noun it modifies, as in "an à la carte menu" or "an à la carte service," or it can follow a linking verb and describe the subject of the sentence, as in "their pricing model is entirely à la carte" or "the options are à la carte." Both uses are equally correct and common.

If you had to capture the whole meaning in one line: something is "à la carte" when it lets you select and pay for individual items from a list, one by one, instead of taking a fixed, pre-packaged set.
